title: 3-Read Friday #62: Retrieval Practice, Assessment, and Edtech
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #62 of 3-Read Friday leads with Carl Hendrick's debut Substack post distilling seven evidence-based principles for implementing retrieval practice well, which Barton calls an incredible summary of the key things teachers need to know. Becky Allen and Matthew Evans then argue that the formative/summative assessment distinction is a false dichotomy -- every assessment must do both jobs, informing teaching and generating valid inferences about attainment, or it fails its underlying purpose of promoting learning. Dan Meyer closes with a pointed rebuttal to Khan Academy's framing of the edtech-teacher relationship, arguing that most edtech doesn't replace teachers so much as waste their accumulated skill by failing to make use of a veteran teacher's experience. Barton highlights Meyer's piece as a reminder that teacher experience -- not AI capability alone -- remains the most impactful lever on student outcomes at this stage of edtech's development.
points: Hendrick's seven-principle retrieval practice framework treats forgetting as a feature (not a bug) of memory consolidation, and warns that same-context retrieval breeds a false sense of mastery that collapses under exam or real-world conditions.

Allen and Evans's core claim -- that the summative/formative split misleads schools into treating high-stakes tests as purely bureaucratic and treating low-stakes checks as exempt from accuracy standards -- reframes assessment design around a single question: how does this assessment help the student learn better?

Meyer's 'wasting teachers' framing gives a concrete diagnostic: if a tool's usefulness doesn't scale with a teacher's years of experience, pedagogical knowledge, or socioemotional skill, it isn't partnering with teachers, it's replacing their judgment with clicks.

Barton's synthesis: at this moment in edtech's evolution, the highest-leverage question isn't whether AI can teach, but whether a given tool makes better use of what experienced teachers already know how to do.
quotes: Carl, one of my favourite education writers, now has a Suvstack!
This is an incredible post summarising the key things teachers need to know to make retrieval practice impactful.
all assessments must be both formative and summative, otherwise, they cannot fulfil their purpose.
The post goes on to confront some less-than-ideal practices that can result from trying to divide tests into formative or summative camps.
I love Dan's musings on the different perspectives of EdTech companies and teachers on the role of AI.

This post is a great reminder of the importance of teacher experience on student outcomes, and what - at this moment in time at least - feels like the most impactful way AI can further improve those outcomes.
